overview: The technical crux of Stuart's North Ridge: a striking 5.8 lieback pitch followed by a 5.9+ offwidth pitch through the 'Great Gendarme,' a prominent rock tower about two-thirds of the way up the ridge; it sits in near-permanent shade and can be cold.
beta: P1 is a lieback (5.8, climbable more directly at 5.9): a few steps of liebacking lead to one final vertical lieback section to the top of the column. P2 is the 'feared' offwidth, easier than its reputation — easy traversing moves on good holds and hand jams (aided by a fixed #1) lead into an easy fist-crack entrance (protectable with a #3), a few fist jams and an armbar to a fixed #4, then easy terrain traversing right.
flagged: This is the crux section of the North Ridge, not a separate route to the summit.

overview: A slender granite spire in the North Cascades backcountry above Stehekin, standing just west of Mount Lyall and linked south to Dark Peak by the jagged, largely unclimbed Anonymity Towers ridge. The peak is not in the Entiat Mountains as earlier described — it rises above the Agnes Creek/Swamp Creek drainage on the west side of Lake Chelan, reached only via the roadless village of Stehekin and the Pacific Crest Trail. It is a rarely-visited, essentially unmaintained scramble/low-5th-class object
beta: Needle Peak sees very few ascents. The standard (and only reported) line leaves the unmaintained Swamp Creek Trail around 3,200 ft, climbs a steep brushy slope to gain the peak's long north ridge near 7,300–7,400 ft, then route-finds through west-facing gullies and krummholz along the ridge before a narrow gully below the overhanging crest, on sloping rock strewn with loose grains, leads to the broad summit.
breakdown: Brushy slope to north ridge: Class 2-3
flagged: The id says south_route but the name, face and beta all describe the North Ridge.

fa: Jim Nelson & Carl Dietrich, 1986 (5.10 A2, with aid); FFA by Max Hasson & Jens Holsten, 2007 (5.11+)
overview: The West Face of North Peak is one of the Cascades' sheerest and cleanest granite faces, offering world-class alpine rock climbing. The route ascends the center of the face with excellent crack and face climbing on solid white granite. Originally established as an aid route in 1986, the first free ascent in 2007 demonstrated the exceptional quality of the line, with sustained 5.11 climbing featuring hard crack work, bulbous knobs, lieback sections, and wild exposure.
beta: A premier alpine testpiece featuring five pitches of high-quality granite climbing to the summit terrace, plus a short sixth pitch up an easy chimney to the summit. The route climbs splitter cracks and exposed face climbing over 600 vertical feet. Pitch 2 contains the crux with thin cracks, bulbous knobs, and a small roof. flagged: Filed under peak 'North Peak' beside Mount Index's North Peak routes, but this is the West Face of North Gunsight Peak in the Gunsight Range.

overview: Pinnacle Peak (6,562 ft) is the signature summit of the Tatoosh Range and by far the most-climbed peak south of Mount Rainier, thanks to a short, spectacular approach from Reflection Lakes. It is not the range's high point — Unicorn Peak (6,971 ft) holds that distinction — but Pinnacle's central position and classic profile make it the classic Tatoosh outing. (accounts disagree on Pinnacle's exact rank: some listings call it the range's second-highest peak, while NPS materials call it third-high
beta: From Pinnacle-Plummer saddle, head east and scramble up obvious gullies on the peak's south side with multiple line options. Stay on most-traveled route for least loose rock. Route-finding is straightforward but exposure increases with altitude. Final push to summit is the steepest and most difficult section, with some variations described as low 5th class.

overview: A short, popular 4th-class scramble up Pinnacle Peak's southwest side, reached from the end of the maintained Pinnacle Saddle Trail. The route follows scree and loose rock roughly along/below the ridge to an obvious chute just east of the peak's westernmost rock prominence, then climbs the chute on progressively steeper, better-cleaned rock to the summit ridge, finishing with a walk to the true summit.
beta: From the saddle, hike/scramble up a mix of scree and loose rock roughly along or below the ridge, following the most-traveled line, to an obvious chute east of the western prominence. The chute climbs on increasingly steep, exposed but better-cleaned rock before topping out near the summit. It is rated 4th class with limited protection options — a few possibilities for slinging horns or trees near the top.

overview: A moderate snow/ice couloir climbing directly to the Balanced Rock at Sherpa's summit, finishing with one short 5.0 rock pitch.

A related pair of unnamed/loosely-named couloirs on the same northeast face have also been skied and climbed, with one reported at over 1,000 ft of continuous climbing.

overview: The West Ridge is the line taken by the 1931 first ascent party and remains the natural finish most climbers use off the Neve Glacier: gain the crest just west of the summit and scramble class 3-4 on gneiss to the top. It isn't a distinct technical line so much as the standard glacier route's summit exit, but it's worth listing separately since older published descriptions treat it as the named route.

fa: William Degenhardt and Herbert Strandberg, August 1931 — this Neve Glacier/West Ridge line is the only historically-documented route to the summit
overview: Snowfield Peak (8,351 ft) is the high point of the Colonial/Neve group in the North Cascades National Park core, about 5 miles ESE of Newhalem. Its defining feature is the roughly 750-acre Neve Glacier draping its north and northwest flanks — one of the larger non-volcanic glaciers in the Washington Cascades — crossed en route to an easy but exposed class 3-4 scramble to the summit.
beta: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead, hike the well-worn trail to Pyramid Lake (~2 mi), then follow a steep, less-traveled climbers' trail up the East Ridge of Pyramid Peak into alpine terrain. Traverse south past the east flank of Paul Bunyan's Stump onto the Colonial Glacier, climb ~30-degree snow to the Colonial-Neve col (~6,800-6,840 ft), then descend roughly 150-250 ft onto the Neve Glacier. Rope up and cross the Neve — parties describe the cleanest line through the center of its crevasse field

overview: The crag's namesake and longest route: a 5-pitch, Grade II trad/sport line that wanders along the line of least resistance up the tallest formation, with a bolted-plus-small-gear crux roof pitch (5.11c) partway up.
beta: P1 follows bolts at 5.10 to chains, then trends left past additional anchor sets. The next section is a corner with traditional gear and a slab. The standout crux pitch is bolted with small trad gear, trending up-right through corners and over a roof (5.11c) to an anchor, after which easier 5.10 slabby climbing leads to the top of the cliff.
